Phoebes are among the earliest flycatchers to arrive in spring, often appearing when there is still snow on the ground, and they habitually pump their tails up and down in a distinctive nervous rhythm. They readily adopt human structures — bridges, barns, porches — as nest sites, returning to the same location year after year.
eastern-phoebe.alt_facts: The eastern phoebe bobs its tail constantly, for reasons it has never explained and which do not appear to be optional. It arrives before spring has fully committed, lands on the nearest fence post, and begins saying its own name in the matter-of-fact way of someone who has been away and is letting the place know it is back.

veery.facts: The veery's song is one of the most ethereal sounds in the eastern forest — a descending, spiraling series of flute-like tones that seem to fold back on themselves, produced by its two-chambered syrinx singing in a kind of self-harmonizing duet. Studies have suggested that veery migration timing and breeding success correlate with Atlantic hurricane activity later in the season, raising the possibility that the birds respond in some way to seasonal cues we do not yet understand. Veeries nest on or just above the ground in moist, shaded forest and are easily overlooked despite their extraordinary voices.
veery.alt_facts: The veery is a small brown bird that opens its mouth and produces a sound that should not come from something this size — a descending spiral, as if the song is made of water and is draining somewhere beautiful. It nests on the ground, completely unbothered, because it knows what it sounds like.

hermit-thrush.facts: The hermit thrush has arguably the most celebrated song of any North American bird — a clear, flute-like opening phrase followed by shimmering harmonics at a different pitch, repeated in ever-varying sequences that can continue for minutes. It is the only spotted thrush that winters in the United States, making it the one thrush reliably heard singing on warm winter days in the South and on early spring mornings farther north. The hermit thrush forages by standing still, then suddenly dropping to snatch invertebrates from leaf litter, using a technique that combines stillness with speed.
hermit-thrush.alt_facts: The hermit thrush stays when the other thrushes leave and sings a song made of several songs nested inside each other, each one a slightly different version of longing. It stands very still in the leaf litter and then moves so fast the stillness was the trick, which describes its whole approach to existing.

northern-parula.facts: The northern parula is a tiny warbler that nests almost exclusively inside clumps of hanging material — Spanish moss in the South, and old man's beard lichen (Usnea) in the North — weaving a small cup inside the hanging strands and pulling them closed around it like a curtain. Its buzzy, rising trill with an abrupt zip at the end is one of the most characteristic sounds of northeastern forests in May. Despite its small size, it winters in the Caribbean and Central America and returns north reliably each spring.
northern-parula.alt_facts: The northern parula finds a curtain of lichen, climbs inside, and closes it behind itself — a bird that has solved the housing problem with a level of elegance the rest of the forest finds slightly show-offy. It has a song that goes up and up and then stops, as if it just thought of something.

blue-headed-vireo.facts: The blue-headed vireo is a deliberate, methodical forager that moves slowly through the canopy, pausing to inspect leaves and twigs with a patience most warblers entirely lack. It is one of the earlier vireos to arrive in spring and one of the latest to leave in fall, with a slow, rich, conversational song it continues singing long after most woodland birds have gone quiet. Its nest is a deep, neatly woven cup suspended from a forked branch and decorated on the outside with bits of lichen, spider silk, and plant down.
blue-headed-vireo.alt_facts: The blue-headed vireo moves through the trees the way someone reads a used bookshop — slowly, with purpose, convinced the right thing is just around the next branch. It has a white eye ring that gives it a permanent expression of polite but firm interest, which is accurate.

eastern-screech-owl.facts: The eastern screech-owl comes in two color morphs — gray and rufous — that are not related to age, sex, or season but appear to be genetically fixed, and both morphs occur throughout the species' range. It is a cavity nester that takes readily to nest boxes and is one of the most common owls in suburban and urban areas of the eastern United States, despite being almost never seen. Its call is not a screech but a long, descending whinny or a trembling, mournful trill — the screech of legend belongs to other species.
eastern-screech-owl.alt_facts: The eastern screech-owl lives inside a tree in your neighborhood and has never once introduced itself. Its name is a lie — it does not screech, it trembles and wails in the dark, which is worse and also better. It exists in two colors for reasons that have been explained to no one's satisfaction.

red-shouldered-hawk.facts: The red-shouldered hawk is a forest hawk of wet woodlands and riparian corridors, often found near streams, swamps, and flooded bottomlands where it hunts frogs, snakes, crayfish, and small mammals. It has a loud, insistent kee-yer call that blue jays famously mimic — possibly to harass other birds at feeders or to test the local hawk situation. Pairs often return to the same nest territory year after year, repairing and reusing the same large stick nest over many seasons.
red-shouldered-hawk.alt_facts: The red-shouldered hawk patrols the wet woods with the air of someone conducting an inspection no one requested. Blue jays have learned its voice and use it without permission, which the hawk has noted and chosen not to dignify with a response.

wood-frog.facts: The wood frog is famous for surviving winter by freezing solid — up to 65 percent of its body water turns to ice, its heart stops, and it stops breathing for months, then thaws and resumes activity in early spring. It is one of the first amphibians to breed each year, descending on vernal pools in large, noisy choruses that can begin while ice is still present at the pool's edges. Wood frogs spend most of their lives on the forest floor far from water, returning to vernal pools only to breed.
wood-frog.alt_facts: The wood frog freezes to death every winter and then reconsiders. It wakes up, walks to the nearest pond, and hollers about it with several hundred friends — which, given what it just went through, seems like a completely proportionate response.

red-eft.facts: The red eft is the terrestrial juvenile stage of the eastern newt — a bright orange-red, land-dwelling phase that can last two to seven years before the newt returns to water and transforms into a drab, aquatic adult. Its vivid color is an honest advertisement: red efts carry potent tetrodotoxin in their skin, the same toxin found in puffer fish, making them genuinely dangerous to eat. They wander forest floors, especially after rain, in plain sight — relying entirely on toxicity rather than camouflage.
red-eft.alt_facts: The red eft is a small poisonous creature that dresses in the brightest color available and walks slowly through the open forest, which is either tremendous confidence or an extremely concise argument. It has decided to be orange for several years and then, without explanation, will change its mind entirely.

pickerel-frog.facts: The pickerel frog is the only truly poisonous frog native to North America — its skin secretions are toxic enough to kill other frogs kept in the same container and can cause irritation in humans who handle it and then touch their eyes or mouth. It is often confused with the leopard frog, but its spots are more rectangular and arranged in two neat parallel rows down the back. Pickerel frogs favor cool, clear streams and spring-fed wetlands and are sometimes considered an indicator of good water quality.
pickerel-frog.alt_facts: The pickerel frog looks exactly like a leopard frog and has nothing to say about the confusion except that the consequences of the confusion are entirely the other party's problem. It keeps its spots in orderly rows, which is the only tidy thing about an animal that is also a mild hazard.

black-throated-blue-warbler.facts: The male black-throated blue warbler is one of the most strikingly plumaged warblers in eastern North America — a deep, navy blue above with a black face and throat and a clean white belly — while the female is so different in appearance, a dull olive-brown, that early ornithologists classified them as separate species. Both sexes carry a small white wing spot, the female's faint but present, which is the reliable field mark linking the pair. Males return to the same breeding territories in Appalachian and northeastern forests year after year with remarkable fidelity.
black-throated-blue-warbler.alt_facts: The male black-throated blue warbler is a bird that has made a decision about color and committed to it fully. The female looks so completely different that for a long time scientists thought they had simply found two birds, which is a reasonable mistake and one the warbler has never bothered to correct.

northern-saw-whet-owl.facts: The northern saw-whet owl is among the smallest owls on the continent — easily fitting in a cupped hand — yet it is a capable predator of mice, voles, and small birds, often caching prey in cold weather and returning to thaw and eat it later. Its repetitive tooting call, given persistently through winter and early spring nights, is far more often heard than the owl is ever seen. Banding studies have revealed that saw-whets migrate in surprisingly large numbers along ridge systems and coastlines, largely invisibly, at night.
northern-saw-whet-owl.alt_facts: The northern saw-whet owl is the size of a large lemon and has the demeanor of something that does not consider this relevant. It calls the same note over and over in the dark for hours, not because it expects an answer, but because it is making a point about the night.

whip-poor-will.facts: The whip-poor-will is a nocturnal, ground-nesting bird that lays its eggs directly on leaf litter — no nest — and times its breeding cycle to coincide with the full moon, using the extra light to forage for the large flying insects it catches entirely on the wing with its enormous, bristle-rimmed mouth. Its camouflage is so complete that a sitting whip-poor-will on a forest floor is nearly invisible even when you are looking directly at it. Populations have declined significantly across the Northeast, likely due to declines in large moth populations and habitat loss.
whip-poor-will.alt_facts: The whip-poor-will lays its eggs on the ground in the dark and trusts that no one will notice, which works, because it is itself indistinguishable from the ground in the dark. It says its own name all night, loudly, in a forest where it cannot be seen, which is a form of confidence that deserves more study.

wood-turtle.facts: The wood turtle is a semi-terrestrial turtle that spends significant time on land, foraging along stream banks and in adjacent meadows and woodlands for berries, mushrooms, worms, and slugs. It has been documented stomping the ground with its plastron to bring earthworms to the surface — a behavior that mimics the vibrations of rain — and then eating them, a level of tool-adjacent problem-solving unusual for reptiles. Wood turtles are long-lived and slow to mature, making their populations particularly vulnerable to adult mortality from road crossings and collection.
wood-turtle.alt_facts: The wood turtle has figured out that if you stomp on the ground correctly, it will produce worms — a discovery it made entirely on its own and has never shared with anyone. It lives a very long time and spends much of it walking slowly between the stream and the meadow with the unhurried confidence of something that has already seen how this goes.

smooth-green-snake.facts: The smooth green snake is one of North America's most docile serpents — a slender, vivid-green hunter that moves through meadow grasses nearly invisible against the stems. It feeds almost entirely on insects and spiders, making it a quiet but effective garden ally. Unlike many snakes, it rarely bites when handled, preferring to rely on camouflage over confrontation.
smooth-green-snake.alt_facts: The smooth green snake is a piece of the lawn that got bored and learned to have opinions. It moves through the grass like a rumor, eating things it finds personally offensive, and is widely regarded among garden snakes as the one most likely to be mistaken for a twig at a dinner party.

spotted-salamander.facts: Spotted salamanders spend most of their lives underground in eastern North American forests, emerging on rainy spring nights to breed in vernal pools — sometimes traveling hundreds of meters in a single night. Their eggs are famously green, tinted by symbiotic algae living inside the egg mass, one of the only known examples of a vertebrate hosting a photosynthesizing organism inside its cells. Adults can live 20 years or more, returning to the same pool every spring.
spotted-salamander.alt_facts: The spotted salamander surfaces once a year on a rainy evening, attends a very important meeting it will not explain, and vanishes back underground for another twelve months. It keeps algae as tiny tenants inside its eggs, which it considers a reasonable arrangement and does not discuss further.

southern-flying-squirrel.facts: The southern flying squirrel doesn't actually fly — it glides on a membrane of skin called the patagium that stretches between its wrists and ankles, covering distances of up to 80 feet in a single leap. It is the smallest tree squirrel in eastern North America and is strictly nocturnal, with enormous dark eyes adapted for low-light navigation. Despite their delicate appearance, these squirrels are surprisingly carnivorous, supplementing nuts and seeds with insects, eggs, and carrion.
southern-flying-squirrel.alt_facts: The southern flying squirrel is a very small creature that has decided the ground is a matter of opinion. It sails through the dark on a built-in cape it never asked for and eats things no one expected it to eat, regarding the whole situation as perfectly normal.

luna-moth.facts: The luna moth is one of North America's largest and most striking moths, with a wingspan reaching up to 4.5 inches and sweeping hindwing tails that researchers believe help deflect bat echolocation away from the body. Adult luna moths have no mouths — they live only about a week, sustained entirely by fat reserves stored during their caterpillar stage, with the sole purpose of finding a mate. Their pale green wings fade in daylight, making them almost ghostly pale by the time they die.
luna-moth.alt_facts: The luna moth emerges already retired, having decided during the caterpillar years that it had eaten enough for one lifetime. It spends its remaining days as a flying piece of sea glass, confusing bats with its decorative tails, and dies having never once opened a bill.

cecropia-moth.facts: The cecropia moth is North America's largest native moth, with a wingspan that can exceed six inches — wide enough to cover an adult human hand. Like the luna moth, cecropia adults have vestigial mouths and cannot eat, surviving their brief adult lives on energy stored as caterpillars. Males can detect a female's pheromones from more than a mile away, navigating by scent alone through a dark forest.
cecropia-moth.alt_facts: The cecropia moth is a stained-glass window the size of a salad plate that has given up on eating and now focuses entirely on being enormous and beautiful in the dark. It finds mates by following a smell it cannot describe across distances it finds unreasonable, which it regards as a perfectly good use of a week.

wheel-bug.facts: The wheel bug is North America's largest assassin bug, named for the dramatic cog-shaped crest on its thorax — a structure whose purpose remains unclear to scientists. It hunts caterpillars, beetles, and other insects by stabbing them with a curved beak and injecting saliva that liquefies their insides, then drinking the result. Despite looking alarming, wheel bugs are shy and slow-moving; a bite to a human, while rare, is reportedly more painful than a wasp sting.
wheel-bug.alt_facts: The wheel bug arrived wearing a gear on its back from a machine no one has ever located, and has been solving that mystery ever since by eating things with a beak shaped like a question mark. It is deeply reclusive for something so architecturally dramatic, and considers its reputation for pain to be both accurate and nobody's business.

bobolink.facts: The bobolink makes one of the longest migrations of any North American songbird, traveling roughly 12,500 miles round-trip between its breeding grounds in northern meadows and its wintering grounds in South America. Males are striking in reverse — dark below, pale on top — and their bubbling, metallic song sounds like a malfunctioning robot tuned to a frequency of pure joy. Bobolinks navigate partly using Earth's magnetic field, with specialized iron-containing cells in their beaks acting as a compass.
bobolink.alt_facts: The bobolink wears its tuxedo upside-down and sings in a language that sounds like a telegraph wire arguing with a music box. It travels 25,000 miles a year simply because it cannot decide which hemisphere it prefers, and navigates with its face, which it finds perfectly efficient.

eastern-meadowlark.facts: The eastern meadowlark is a stocky grassland bird whose bright yellow chest and bold black V-shaped bib make it instantly recognizable — though it is technically a blackbird, not a lark. Its flute-like song, often described as clear and whistled, carries across open fields and has been declining along with the grassland habitat the species depends on. Meadowlarks build their nests on the ground, often weaving a woven dome of grass over the cup to conceal it from above.
eastern-meadowlark.alt_facts: The eastern meadowlark is wearing a formal waistcoat in a field where no one asked it to dress up, and it is singing anyway, loudly, because it has things to say about fields in general. Its nest is a small thatched cottage with a grass roof, which it considers both structurally sound and nobody's business.

golden-winged-warbler.facts: The golden-winged warbler is a small, precisely patterned songbird — gray above with a blazing yellow crown and wing patch and a sharp black mask — that nests in shrubby, early-successional habitat that is rapidly disappearing across eastern North America. It hybridizes extensively with the blue-winged warbler where their ranges overlap, producing fertile offspring called Brewster's and Lawrence's warblers, complicating conservation efforts. Populations have declined steeply, making it one of the most at-risk warblers on the continent.
golden-winged-warbler.alt_facts: The golden-winged warbler is a small bird wearing a painter's cap and a bandit mask, which together send a mixed message it has never bothered to resolve. It occasionally marries into another family and produces children with entirely different names, which it finds administratively confusing but emotionally fine.

northern-goshawk.facts: The northern goshawk is the largest and most formidable of North America's accipiters — a forest hawk built for speed and agility among dense trees, capable of twisting through tight woodland at full chase velocity. Its slate-gray plumage, fierce red eye, and bold white eyebrow stripe give it an expression that naturalists have consistently described as furious. Goshawks defend their nests with extraordinary aggression, regularly striking human intruders hard enough to draw blood.
northern-goshawk.alt_facts: The northern goshawk is a bird that flies through forests the way an argument moves through a quiet room — fast, committed, and leaving a strong impression. It has the expression of someone who has heard your excuse already and found it insufficient, and it nests with the conviction of a creature that has never once been wrong.

olive-sided-flycatcher.facts: The olive-sided flycatcher is a stocky, large-headed bird of northern coniferous forests, named for the dark olive patches along its sides that frame a white belly like an unbuttoned vest. Its three-note song — commonly transcribed as quick-three-beers — is one of the most recognizable sounds of boreal summer. It is a long-distance migrant, wintering in South America, and has declined significantly due to habitat loss on both ends of its range.
olive-sided-flycatcher.alt_facts: The olive-sided flycatcher perches at the very tip of the tallest dead tree available, surveys its entire territory, and announces its opinion in three emphatic syllables it repeats without apology until everyone has heard it. It dresses like it started getting changed and then decided this was enough.

northern-long-eared-bat.facts: The northern long-eared bat is a small, forest-dependent bat with distinctly long ears it uses for precise echolocation, allowing it to detect and pluck insects directly from foliage — a technique called gleaning that few bats attempt. It roosts under bark and in tree cavities during summer, often alone or in small maternity colonies. White-nose syndrome, caused by a fungal pathogen introduced from Europe, has decimated its populations, leading to federal listing as an endangered species.
northern-long-eared-bat.alt_facts: The northern long-eared bat has ears it clearly grew into and uses them to hear things in the dark that are technically not making any sound yet. It sleeps in trees one at a time, takes its roosting very seriously, and has been through a great deal, which it handles with the quiet dignity of something that hunts in complete darkness and still doesn't miss.

tricolored-bat.facts: The tricolored bat — formerly called the eastern pipistrelle — is one of the smallest bats in eastern North America, weighing only about as much as a penny. Its name comes from the banding of color on its individual fur hairs: dark at the base, pale in the middle, and tipped in brown. It is often the first bat seen flying in the evening, emerging before other species while there is still light in the sky, and it has been severely affected by white-nose syndrome.
tricolored-bat.alt_facts: The tricolored bat weighs less than a coin and has decided this is no obstacle to having a very full evening. Each of its hairs is wearing three colors simultaneously in a gradient arrangement that serves no purpose it has chosen to explain. It shows up to dusk before anyone else, which it considers punctual and others consider excessive.

new-england-cottontail.facts: The New England cottontail is the region's only native rabbit species — and it looks nearly identical to the introduced eastern cottontail, which has largely displaced it across southern New England. It can only be reliably told apart by examining its skull or via DNA testing, a situation the two species do not appear to find awkward. The New England cottontail requires dense, shrubby thicket habitat for cover and has declined steeply as that habitat has been lost to development and forest maturation.
new-england-cottontail.alt_facts: The New England cottontail has a cousin who moved in from elsewhere and looks exactly like it, and the only way anyone can officially tell them apart is to ask a scientist with a laboratory, which the rabbits consider a disproportionate response. It lives in the thickest, most impenetrable brush it can find, which it regards as a reasonable policy.

blandings-turtle.facts: Blanding's turtle is a medium-sized freshwater turtle with a domed, helmet-like shell and a bright yellow chin and throat that make it recognizable at a glance. It is remarkably long-lived — individuals have been documented past 70 years old — and does not reach reproductive maturity until its mid-teens, making population recovery from declines extremely slow. It relies on a mosaic of wetlands and upland habitat, traveling overland between seasonal wetlands, which brings it into frequent conflict with roads.
blandings-turtle.alt_facts: The Blanding's turtle has a yellow chin it wears like a small, permanent smile, and it has been wearing it for possibly seventy years without complaint. It crosses roads with the calm confidence of something that was here long before the road arrived and fully expects to outlast it.

marbled-salamander.facts: The marbled salamander is a stocky, boldly patterned mole salamander with crisp white or silver crossbands on a black body — one of the most striking salamanders in eastern North America. Unlike most of its relatives, it breeds in autumn rather than spring, with females laying eggs in dry woodland depressions and guarding them until autumn rains fill the site with water. It spends the vast majority of its life underground or beneath logs, rarely seen despite being locally common.
marbled-salamander.alt_facts: The marbled salamander dresses in formal black-and-white stripes and guards its eggs in what is currently a dry hole, on the understanding that eventually the rain will come and prove it right. It lives almost entirely underground and considers visibility an overrated quality in a salamander.

rusty-patched-bumblebee.facts: The rusty-patched bumblebee was once one of the most common bumblebees in eastern North America; it is now federally listed as endangered — the first bee placed on the U.S. endangered species list. The rusty patch that gives the species its name is a small reddish-orange smudge on the abdomen of workers and males, not found on queens. Its decline has been driven by habitat loss, pesticides, and disease, and it has vanished from roughly 90 percent of its former range.
rusty-patched-bumblebee.alt_facts: The rusty-patched bumblebee carries a small rust-colored mark like a drop of something it ran into once and never quite got out, and it has been through a great deal since then. It used to be everywhere, and its continued presence in the places it still visits is both a fact and a small, ongoing miracle it does not make a fuss about.

puritan-tiger-beetle.facts: The Puritan tiger beetle is a federally threatened insect found only on a handful of sandy riverbank and coastal beach sites along the Connecticut River and the Chesapeake Bay. Like other tiger beetles, it is a fast and voracious predator with large eyes and powerful jaws, capable of running so quickly it must temporarily blind itself mid-sprint because its visual system can't keep pace. Its larvae dig vertical burrows in the sand and ambush prey from the entrance.
puritan-tiger-beetle.alt_facts: The Puritan tiger beetle runs faster than its own eyes can process and does not let this stop it — it simply closes them mid-chase and recalculates on the other side. It lives on a short list of specific sandy riverbanks it has approved, and it has approved very few.

frosted-elfin.facts: The frosted elfin is a small, early-spring butterfly with subtle gray-brown wings and a delicate frosted appearance on the hindwing undersides that gives it its name. It is a specialist, with caterpillars feeding only on wild lupine or wild indigo, and populations are tightly tied to the presence of these host plants in open, sandy habitats. It is one of the first butterflies of spring, flying for only a few weeks in April and May before disappearing for the year.
frosted-elfin.alt_facts: The frosted elfin appears for a few weeks in early spring, accomplishes everything it came to do, and leaves before anyone has entirely registered it was there. It has strong opinions about lupine and will not negotiate on this point.

common-eastern-bumblebee.facts: The common eastern bumblebee is one of the most frequently seen bumblebees across eastern North America, with a yellow and black pattern and the characteristic dense fuzz that helps it warm up its flight muscles in cool weather — allowing it to forage on cold days when other pollinators stay home. Colonies are annual: a single mated queen overwinters, founds a new nest in spring, and the colony grows through summer before dying back in autumn. It is a native bee and a generalist pollinator, visiting hundreds of plant species.
common-eastern-bumblebee.alt_facts: The common eastern bumblebee is furry for a reason it will explain if you let it get to the point, which is that cold weather is not an excuse. It shows up to flowers when no one else has bothered, does the work, and leaves without ceremony. The queen survives winter alone and considers this a reasonable arrangement.

eastern-carpenter-bee.facts: Eastern carpenter bees look strikingly like bumblebees but have a shiny, bare black abdomen rather than a fuzzy one — a useful field mark. Females excavate perfectly round tunnels in unpainted wood, creating galleries where they lay eggs provisioned with pollen; the same tunnels may be reused and extended for years. Despite their intimidating size, males — the ones that hover aggressively in your face — have no stingers at all, while females sting only if physically restrained.
eastern-carpenter-bee.alt_facts: The male eastern carpenter bee has made a career of hovering directly in people's faces with tremendous confidence despite being completely unarmed, which is either very brave or a fundamental misunderstanding of the situation. The female, who can actually sting, drills perfect circles in wood and finds the whole performance embarrassing.

paper-wasp.facts: Paper wasps build their iconic open-celled, umbrella-shaped nests from wood fibers they chew into a gray papery pulp — each hexagonal cell housing a single larva fed on chewed caterpillars and other insects. Unlike yellowjackets or hornets, paper wasp nests are not enclosed in an outer envelope, and colonies are relatively small, rarely exceeding a few dozen individuals. They are important predators of garden caterpillars and generally non-aggressive unless their nest is directly disturbed.
paper-wasp.alt_facts: The paper wasp invented the hexagon independently and uses it to raise children in open rooms it has no intention of finishing — no roof, no insulation, full exposure to inspection, no apologies. It hunts caterpillars to feed its family, which is both ecologically useful and something the caterpillars did not vote for.

hover-fly.facts: Hover flies are masters of aerial stillness, able to hold a fixed position in midair with wingbeats so fast they become invisible — then vanish and reappear feet away in an instant. Many species are bee or wasp mimics, wearing yellow-and-black stripes despite being completely harmless, a strategy called Batesian mimicry. Adults feed on nectar and pollen and are significant pollinators, while larvae of many species eat aphids, making hover flies doubly useful in the garden.
hover-fly.alt_facts: The hover fly dresses as a wasp with the full knowledge that it has no venom and a great deal of confidence. It hangs in the air doing nothing, perfectly, for longer than seems reasonable, and then leaves. Its children eat aphids, which it regards as a sensible division of family labor.

bald-faced-hornet.facts: The bald-faced hornet is actually a yellowjacket, not a true hornet — the only North American member of its genus, distinguished by its white-and-black face. Its paper nests, built from chewed wood pulp, can reach the size of a basketball or larger by late summer, housing hundreds of workers. It is an aggressive defender of its nest and can sting repeatedly, but is an effective predator of caterpillars, flies, and other insects when foraging away from home.
bald-faced-hornet.alt_facts: The bald-faced hornet builds a gray paper globe the size of a sports equipment malfunction and fills it with opinions about proximity. It has a white face it wears like a mask at a party it is also hosting and also catering, exclusively with things it has caught.

mud-dauber-wasp.facts: Mud dauber wasps are solitary wasps that construct distinctive tubular nests from wet mud, provisioning each cell with paralyzed spiders before sealing it with an egg inside. Unlike social wasps, mud daubers have no colony to defend and are remarkably docile — stings are extremely rare and occur only under direct handling. Several species specifically target black widow spiders, making them an unlikely but effective ally in the garden.
mud-dauber-wasp.alt_facts: The mud dauber wasp builds an apartment out of wet dirt, stuffs each room with a paralyzed spider it has personally evaluated, lays one egg, seals the door, and considers itself an excellent parent. It does this alone, with no help, and has no interest in stinging anyone about it.

great-golden-digger-wasp.facts: The great golden digger wasp is a large, striking solitary wasp with a golden-orange abdomen and black-and-gold markings, often seen nectaring conspicuously on flowers in late summer. Females excavate burrows in sandy soil and stock them with paralyzed katydids and crickets, each one carefully stung into immobility and dragged back to provision an egg. Despite their size, great golden digger wasps are gentle and rarely sting; males cannot sting at all.
great-golden-digger-wasp.alt_facts: The great golden digger wasp is enormous, festively colored, and drags crickets three times its own body weight across the yard with the focused energy of someone who has made a list and intends to complete it. It visits flowers with the same intensity it brings to everything, which is considerable, and it cannot be talked out of any of this.

leafcutter-bee.facts: Leafcutter bees cut precise semicircular pieces from leaves and petals — not to eat, but to line the cylindrical nest cells where they provision each egg with a ball of pollen and nectar. Unlike honeybees, they are solitary: every female is her own queen, her own worker, and her own architect. They are exceptionally efficient pollinators, often outperforming honeybees on crops like alfalfa and blueberries because they carry dry pollen loosely on their abdomens rather than packed tight in baskets.
leafcutter-bee.alt_facts: The leafcutter bee is a small upholsterer who has never once been asked her opinion and has decided to wallpaper every room anyway. She collects fabric samples from the garden's finest roses and carries them home in her arms, which she uses for everything because she has decided pockets are for other bees.

garden-snail.facts: The garden snail carries its shell for life — the shell grows with it, added to in rings like a tree, and is made largely of calcium the snail extracts from soil and stone. A snail moves on a single muscular foot, gliding on a self-secreted mucus that reduces friction so effectively the snail can slide across a razor's edge without injury. They are hermaphrodites, each individual carrying both reproductive systems, though they still seek a partner to mate.
garden-snail.alt_facts: The garden snail is a philosopher who has committed fully to the idea that speed is a failure of imagination. It carries its house everywhere because it learned long ago that landlords are unreliable, and leaves a silver signature across every stone it passes — a memoir no one asked for and no one can stop.

american-marten.facts: The American marten is a small, agile mustelid of northern and montane forests, closely associated with old-growth stands of spruce and fir where fallen logs and dense canopy provide both prey and refuge from predators. It hunts voles, squirrels, and birds with quick, bounding efficiency and caches food in winter. Trapping pressure and habitat loss eliminated martens from most of New England and the mid-Atlantic by the early twentieth century, though reintroduction efforts have returned small populations to some of their former range.
american-marten.alt_facts: The marten is a footnote that grew legs and went back into the woods to see if anyone would notice. It moves through old forest like a rumor — quick, brown, and gone before the sentence is finished — and it has been doing this since before your grandfather's grandfather thought to look.

eastern-wolf.facts: The eastern wolf — sometimes called the Algonquin wolf — was a distinct canid of the northeastern forests, likely a close relative of the red wolf rather than a simple variant of the gray wolf. It was smaller than the gray wolf and appears to have specialized in white-tailed deer. Relentless persecution eliminated it from the contiguous United States, and even in Canada its range has collapsed to a few protected pockets around Algonquin Provincial Park, where hybridization with coyotes clouds the edges of what it was.
eastern-wolf.alt_facts: The eastern wolf howled for so long into forests that kept getting smaller that the forests eventually forgot to howl back. It left behind a shape in the dark between the trees — not quite wolf, not quite memory — that the deer still seem to remember on cold nights, even now.

passenger-pigeon.facts: The passenger pigeon was once the most numerous bird in North America, with flocks estimated in the billions that darkened the sky for hours and broke tree branches under their collective weight when they roosted. They were hunted commercially with industrial ferocity in the nineteenth century — netted, shot, and shipped to city markets by the barrel — and the last individual, a female named Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. A species that had seemed as permanent as the sky itself was gone in a single human lifetime.
passenger-pigeon.alt_facts: The passenger pigeon was the sky's way of showing off — a billion birds moving as one dark river overhead, blotting the sun for the pure theater of it. Now there is only the one September afternoon, quiet, in Cincinnati, which the sky has never quite gotten over.

heath-hen.facts: The heath hen was a subspecies of the greater prairie-chicken that once ranged across the coastal heathlands and scrub oak barrens of the eastern seaboard from New England to Virginia. Hunting and habitat loss confined the last population to Martha's Vineyard, where a 1916 brush fire and a brutal winter nearly finished them; the last individual was seen on March 11, 1932. Conservation efforts for the heath hen were among the earliest serious attempts at saving a North American bird from extinction — and they failed, by a margin too narrow to forget.
heath-hen.alt_facts: The heath hen stayed on its island long after the island stopped being enough, as if stubbornness alone might negotiate with arithmetic. The last one walked the scrub oak barrens for years after it should have been impossible, until one morning it decided that was enough — and it was.

eastern-wild-turkey-ghost.alt_facts: The eastern wild turkey ghost is not extinct — it is simply offended and has gone translucent about it. It haunts the edge of the wood line at dusk, dragging its iridescent tail through the goldenrod, leaving three-toed prints in the frost that stop, inexplicably, in the middle of a field. Local tradition holds that if you hear gobbling from a direction where no turkey could possibly be, you owe it an apology.

eastern-elk.facts: The eastern elk — also called the wapiti of the eastern forests — was a large subspecies that ranged across the deciduous woodlands of the eastern United States and southern Canada before European settlement. They were hunted to extinction in the eastern states by the mid-1800s, the last confirmed individuals in Pennsylvania gone by around 1867. The elk found in Pennsylvania today are descended from Rocky Mountain elk reintroduced in the early twentieth century — a stand-in for something that can no longer stand for itself.
eastern-elk.alt_facts: The eastern elk was the forest's largest opinion — a thousand pounds of antler and intention moving through the hardwoods like a sentence that takes all day to finish. The woods remember the weight of it in the way old trails still run deeper than anything alive now has any reason to have made.

woodland-caribou.facts: Woodland caribou were the only member of the deer family in which both sexes grow antlers — an adaptation thought to help females compete for feeding craters in snow. They ranged through the boreal forests of New England and the Great Lakes region but were extirpated from the contiguous United States by the early twentieth century through a combination of hunting, habitat loss, and the expansion of white-tailed deer, which carry a brain worm fatal to caribou. A few individuals still occasionally cross the border from Canada into Maine, where they are met with the particular attention reserved for things that have no business still existing.
woodland-caribou.alt_facts: The woodland caribou wore its antlers like an overcommitment — both sexes, all winter, through the snow — and moved through the northern forest as if it had somewhere to be that turned out not to be here anymore. It left behind its trails, which the moose use now without acknowledgment.

wild-atlantic-salmon.facts: Wild Atlantic salmon once filled the rivers of New England in such numbers that colonial-era accounts describe servants petitioning to be fed salmon no more than three times a week. They navigate thousands of miles of open ocean and return — using magnetic fields and the scent memory of their birth river — to spawn in the exact tributary where they hatched. Dams, pollution, and overfishing collapsed populations throughout their southern range; the Connecticut River's salmon are functionally extinct as a self-sustaining run, and the few remaining wild fish in US rivers cling on with heavy intervention.
wild-atlantic-salmon.alt_facts: The wild Atlantic salmon memorizes the smell of home as a fingerling and carries that memory across the entire ocean and back, which is either the most romantic thing in the natural world or a demonstration of what happens when you refuse to let anything go. It leaps waterfalls on the way home because of course it does.

sea-mink.facts: The sea mink was the largest mink ever known, native to the rocky coasts of the Gulf of Maine and Maritime Canada, where it hunted fish and crustaceans among the intertidal ledges. It was larger and reportedly more aggressive than the American mink and had a distinctly reddish, coarser fur that made it a target for the pelt trade. It was hunted to extinction sometime in the late nineteenth century — the exact date is unknown because it was never formally described by science before it disappeared; what we know of it comes almost entirely from bones in Indigenous shell middens and the recollections of trappers.
sea-mink.alt_facts: The sea mink was big, red, and entirely unimpressed by the fact that no naturalist ever got around to writing it down before it was gone. It is the only animal in the region that managed to go extinct without ever officially existing, which it would have found irritating if it had been consulted.

great-auk.facts: The great auk was a large, flightless seabird of the North Atlantic — the original 'penguin,' a name later applied to the unrelated southern birds by sailors who recognized the silhouette. It was an extraordinary diver, propelling itself underwater with its wings to catch fish at depth, but its inability to fly and its habit of nesting in dense, accessible colonies made it catastrophically vulnerable to human hunters. The last known pair was killed on Eldey Island, Iceland, on June 3, 1844 — their egg crushed in the process — by collectors working on behalf of a museum that wanted a specimen before there were no more specimens to have.
great-auk.alt_facts: The great auk decided that flight was unnecessary and was correct about everything except the part where that mattered. It stood upright on North Atlantic rocks for millennia, diving deeper than seemed reasonable and returning with fish, until the day a museum decided it needed one more than the ocean did.

labrador-duck.facts: The Labrador duck holds the distinction of being the first North American bird to go extinct after the United States was founded, vanishing sometime around 1875 — and it did so before anyone fully understood where it bred, what it ate, or why it was disappearing. Its bill was unusual for a duck, soft and expanded at the tip in a way that suggested a specialized diet, possibly shellfish in coastal estuaries, but no one documented its nesting grounds before it was gone. Only fifty-five museum specimens exist, which is nearly everything we know of it.
labrador-duck.alt_facts: The Labrador duck left before anyone thought to ask it any questions, which is either deeply rude or deeply wise depending on your opinion of questions. Fifty-five museums keep a piece of it under glass, and it tells them nothing, which is exactly as much as it told anyone while it was alive.

eskimo-curlew.facts: The Eskimo curlew was a small shorebird that once migrated in enormous flocks from its Arctic breeding grounds down through the Great Plains and on to the pampas of South America — a journey of thousands of miles, made twice a year. Hunters shot them by the wagonload during migration, and the conversion of prairie to agriculture eliminated the berry-rich stopover habitat the birds depended on to refuel. The last widely accepted sighting was in 1963; a handful of subsequent reports remain unconfirmed, and the species is almost certainly gone, though it has never been formally declared extinct.
eskimo-curlew.alt_facts: The Eskimo curlew flew from one end of the hemisphere to the other twice a year and did it in flocks so thick they were called a 'dough bird' because you could shape the flock with your hands — which is the kind of thing someone said who had never considered what would happen if the hands kept reaching. It may or may not still be out there. The paperwork hasn't decided.

carolina-parakeet.facts: The Carolina parakeet was the only parrot native to the eastern United States, a bright-plumed, noisy, sociable bird that ranged from the Great Lakes to the Gulf Coast before its population collapsed in the nineteenth century. It was shot relentlessly — as an agricultural pest, for its feathers, and simply because flocks of parrots were irresistible targets — and its social nature worked against it: flocks would circle back over fallen companions, making them easy to shoot in waves. The last known individual, a male named Incas, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on February 21, 1918, in the same cage that had held the last passenger pigeon four years earlier.
carolina-parakeet.alt_facts: The Carolina parakeet was a primary-color argument that the eastern forest was in fact a jungle, and it made this argument loudly, in flocks, at every possible opportunity. When one fell the rest came back to say something about it, which was loyal and terrible and very, very parakeet.

eastern-cougar.facts: The eastern cougar was declared officially extinct by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in 2011, though debate persists about whether it was ever truly a distinct subspecies or simply the westernmost overlap of the mountain lion's range. Cougars were systematically hunted out of the eastern United States by the late 1800s; the last confirmed resident eastern population survived in Florida as the Florida panther. What keeps the eastern cougar alive as a concept is the steady trickle of sightings across New England and the mid-Atlantic — most attributable to dispersing western mountain lions — and the stubborn human sense that something big and quiet is still moving through the old woods.
eastern-cougar.alt_facts: The eastern cougar is officially extinct, which it treats as a bureaucratic technicality. Hunters, hikers, and people driving backroads at dusk keep seeing something large and tawny that shouldn't be there, which the cougar finds gratifying. It has not returned anyone's calls.

melanistic-bobcat.facts: The bobcat is the most widespread wild cat in North America and lives across a broad range of habitats, from boreal forests to desert scrub. Melanism — the genetic condition producing an all-black or very dark coat — occurs in several wild cat species but has never been confirmed by specimen or photograph in North American bobcats, despite persistent reports from hunters and trackers in the eastern states. Whether melanistic bobcats exist as rare individuals or whether the sightings reflect misidentification of other dark animals remains genuinely unresolved.
melanistic-bobcat.alt_facts: The melanistic bobcat is either a rare genetic marvel or the bobcat's greatest act of performance art — it shows up in enough convincing stories to be taken seriously and in enough unverifiable accounts to remain deniable. Black cats have always known how to work a room.

wolverine.facts: The wolverine is the largest terrestrial mustelid, built like a small bear and famously capable of driving wolves and mountain lions from their kills despite weighing no more than a large domestic dog. It requires vast, remote territories — a single animal may range over hundreds of square miles — and is highly dependent on persistent spring snowpack for denning. Wolverines were extirpated from the contiguous United States through the twentieth century but have been slowly recolonizing parts of the northern Rockies; occasional confirmed sightings in the Great Lakes region and, rarely, New England suggest that the edge of their range may still brush the Northeast.
wolverine.alt_facts: The wolverine is pound-for-pound the most aggressive argument in the forest, and it knows it. Every few years one turns up somewhere in the Northeast where wolverines have no business being, looks around at whatever is there, decides it's not impressed, and leaves — which is exactly what a wolverine would do.

white-squirrel.facts: White squirrels — leucistic or truly albino gray squirrels — occur as rare natural variants throughout the gray squirrel's range, but several towns in the eastern United States have established colonies where the white form has become locally common through a combination of genetic drift and, in some cases, active protection from hunting. Leucistic individuals lack most pigment but retain dark eyes, while true albinos have pink eyes and often suffer from vision and other health problems. In areas without heavy predation pressure, the white coat's conspicuousness becomes less of a liability, and the population can tip toward pale.
white-squirrel.alt_facts: The white squirrel is a gray squirrel that had a thought and hasn't been the same since. In certain towns it has become so common that it is the normal one, and the gray squirrels are the ones people stop to photograph, which the white squirrel finds entirely appropriate.

lake-monster-champ.alt_facts: Champ has lived in Lake Champlain since before Vermont and New York agreed on where the lake's edges were, which it finds irrelevant. It surfaces occasionally — long neck, dark back, the specific shape of something that shouldn't be there — and then it goes back down, because it has made its point. Both states have passed resolutions protecting it, which Champ acknowledges by continuing to exist on its own terms.

pukwudgie.alt_facts: The pukwudgie is a small, grey-skinned being of Wampanoag tradition — roughly human-shaped but its own kind entirely — with a deep and well-documented grievance against being bothered. It is said to appear in the Bridgewater Triangle and along the old paths of southeastern Massachusetts, usually to travelers who would have been better served by staying home. It can appear and disappear at will, which it exercises freely, and it has no interest in explaining itself.

dover-demon.alt_facts: The Dover Demon appeared on three consecutive nights in April 1977 in Dover, Massachusetts — pale, large-eyed, moving along a stone wall with its long fingers trailing — and then never again, which suggests it had somewhere to be and got there. Four teenagers saw it independently, drew roughly the same thing, and agreed on the detail no one plans for: it looked back.

glawackus.alt_facts: The glawackus terrorized Glastonbury, Connecticut in January 1939 — a large, dark, cat-like creature that screamed in the night and left tracks in the snow that the newspaper reported with the seriousness reserved for things that cannot be explained by noon. Hunters went out. They found nothing. The glawackus, for its part, never clarified what it was, where it came from, or where it went, and Connecticut has had to live with that.

gloucester-sea-serpent.alt_facts: The Gloucester sea serpent has been reported in Massachusetts Bay since at least 1638, which means it has outlasted most of the institutions that have tried to debunk it. It is described as enormously long, dark, and possessed of a series of humps — like a string of barrels, said the fishermen, who are not given to exaggeration about the sea. The Linnaean Society of New England commissioned a formal investigation in 1817 and concluded something was out there, then said no more about it, which is its own kind of answer.

pioneer-valley-visitor.alt_facts: The Pioneer Valley Visitor does not have an agreed-upon shape, which it considers a feature. It has been reported moving through the tobacco fields and river bottomlands of the Connecticut River Valley as a large, dark, shambling thing — sometimes near Northampton, sometimes near Deerfield, always at dusk, always retreating before anyone can be sure. Local naturalists note that the valley's geography funnels wildlife unexpectedly, but local naturalists were also not the ones who saw it.

memphre.alt_facts: Memphre lives in Lake Memphremagog, which straddles the Vermont-Quebec border, and has therefore never been required to declare a country of residence. It has been reported since at least the early 1800s — long-necked, dark, surfacing quietly near the middle of the lake where the water goes very deep very fast. In 1996 a local diver registered it with the International Society of Cryptozoology, giving Memphre the distinction of being perhaps the only lake monster with a file.
